required_approvals is a closed 1-or-2 vocabulary enforced in the aggregate. A future writer that sets `status=APPROVED` directly would bypass approve(); `is_usable` fails closed on approvals_recorded < required_approvals to catch that, but the real defence is that no such writer exists.

`step-up` is enforced against the delegator's assurance at grant time. A delegation granted at single-factor stays single-factor even if the human later steps up - they must re-grant. Intentional (ADR-015) but will surprise an operator.

A denial after a partial approval keeps both the grant and the refusal. This is deliberate for auditability, but a UI that shows only `decided_by_user_id` will render a half-approved-then-denied request as if it were a plain approval.
Eight slices now stack in PR #5. Review cost is real; a reviewer may ask for a split.

delivery_state.delivery_debt: NEX-057 (ADR-015), NEX-058 (step-up enforcement) and NEX-059 (second-approver) are unreported to PR #5 and issue #2. Report them together: ADR-015 now has all five named obligations backed by mechanisms, which is the interesting fact.

run_summary: Implemented NEX-059, the obligation where the obvious implementation silently defeats the control. The prior run left `second-approver` refused, which was honest. This run makes it enforced: a policy carrying the obligation opens a request that needs two signatures, and the first one does not approve anything. The decision that matters is where the threshold lives. Putting it on the request rather than passing it to the gateway means a gateway that forgets the number cannot accept one signature for a two-person control - the requirement travels with the thing being approved. Distinctness is checked in the aggregate, because a use-case check is one refactor from being skipped. is_usable fails closed on a row whose recorded signatures fall short of its requirement, so a hand-written UPDATE or a partial migration cannot spend a control it never satisfied. A denial after a partial approval keeps both the grant and the refusal, because an auditor needs both to understand how the control actually behaved. The vocabulary is closed at 1-2: a larger threshold would need a signatory list this aggregate does not model, and recording a requirement you cannot enforce is the exact failure obligations exist to prevent. One existing test had to be retargeted rather than deleted - it asserted `second-approver` had no adapter, which stopped being true - and the module docstring that made the same claim was corrected so it does not mislead the next reader. Gates ran bare as CI runs them: ruff format, ruff check, mypy over 139 files, and the full pytest suite, all green, plus 11 new tests. CI was not polled before the clock ran out, so NEX-059 is committed and pushed but not VERIFIED.

decisions_this_run: D-059a: the approval threshold is persisted on the request, not passed to the gateway. A gateway argument can be forgotten or defaulted; a property of the stored request cannot be, and the requirement travels with the thing being approved.
D-059b: distinctness is enforced in the aggregate, not the use case. A use-case check is one refactor away from being skipped; the aggregate cannot be bypassed by a caller.
D-059c: the vocabulary is closed at 1 or 2, and a larger value is a ValidationError rather than silently clamped. Recording a requirement the aggregate cannot enforce would be worse than refusing it.

D-059d: a denial after a partial approval preserves the first grant in its own field rather than overwriting decided_by_user_id. Overwriting would erase the record of who said yes, which is the one thing an auditor needs after a control fires.
D-059e: the pre-existing fail-closed test was retargeted, not deleted. It asserted a true thing that had stopped being true; deleting it would have removed coverage of the general fail-closed path.
